# Install cuPhoton {#sec-install}

cuPhoton installs from a source checkout. CPU workflows need no GPU. The GPU profile targets CUDA 13 and an NVIDIA driver that supports it. The repository's [getting-started guide](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuPhoton/blob/main/docs/getting-started.md) has the full list of profiles and platform notes.

**You need:** CPython 3.12 to 3.14 on Linux, Git, and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), the supported environment tool.

## Clone the repository

```bash
git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuPhoton.git
cd cuPhoton
```

This clones the development branch, which this guide describes. To use a published version instead, pick its tag from [Releases](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuPhoton/releases), add `--branch TAG` to the clone command, and use the documentation in that checkout.

## Choose a profile

A profile is a set of extras. Pick the line that matches your machine:

```bash
# CPU only: PyTorch, photometry, xImage and the catalog tables that several pages read
uv sync --locked --extra ximage --extra catalog

# NVIDIA GPU with CUDA 13: adds the GPU readers and CUDA PyTorch
uv sync --locked --extra gpu --extra ximage --extra catalog
```

Add an extra for each optional workflow:

| Extra | Adds | Needed for |
|---|---|---|
| `torch` | PyTorch on the CPU | xScan and xImage without a GPU |
| `photometry` | Photutils | source detection and aperture photometry |
| `gpu` | CuPy, nvCOMP, KvikIO, Photutils, CUDA PyTorch | every GPU path |
| `ximage` | PyTorch, Photutils, Pydantic and Zarr | xImage configurations and bundles |
| `catalog` | Pandas and NumExpr | xScan catalogs, the transient-chain example and the pages that read tables with Pandas |
| `mpi` | mpi4py (bring your own MPI runtime) | MPI executors (@sec-scale) |
| `dragon` | DragonHPC, Python 3.12 or 3.13 only. `make sync-dragon` builds a Dragon environment | Dragon executors (@sec-scale) |
| `viz` | Bokeh and Pillow | interactive views |

The figures in this guide also need Matplotlib, which no profile installs. Add it after you sync with `uv pip install matplotlib`.

List every extra you want in one `uv sync` call. A later call without an extra removes it. `uv sync` also removes packages you added with `uv pip install`, such as the transient-chain example (@sec-transient-chain). Reinstall them after each sync.

To install into an existing environment with pip instead, run `python -m pip install -e '.[ximage,catalog]'` from the checkout. The lock file covers Linux only. On macOS, `uv sync --locked` fails, and the CPU profile installs with this pip command.

The native GPU FITS reader (xDR) needs a separate source build even with the `gpu` profile. Refer to the [xDR install notes](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuPhoton/blob/main/docs/components/xdr.md#install). Without it, cuPhoton reads FITS files with Astropy.

The `native` backends of xRep, xPois and xFit (@sec-concepts), and xDR's `native` pixel restoration (@sec-read-fits), need the `gpu` profile and cuPhoton's native extension. A checkout builds the extension only when you set `CUPHOTON_XFIT_BUILD_EXT=1`. The build needs Linux, a CUDA 13 toolkit with cuBLAS, cuSOLVER and cuFFT, and a C++17 compiler. Refer to the [native xFit build notes](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuPhoton/blob/main/docs/components/xfit.md#optional-native-cuda-backend).

## Check the installation

Run these from the checkout:

```bash
uv run --no-sync python -c "import cuphoton; print(cuphoton.__version__)"
uv run --no-sync cuphoton --help
```

The first command prints the version. The second lists the command groups, one per module:

```{python}
#| echo: false
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

cli = Path(sys.executable).with_name("cuphoton")
print(subprocess.run([str(cli), "--help"], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip())
```

To exercise every module on small generated inputs, run the repository's smoke test. Each run needs a new output directory:

```bash
uv run --no-sync python examples/run_quickstarts.py --profile cpu --output-dir /tmp/cuphoton-quickstart
```

On a GPU host, add `--require-gpu` to fail instead of falling back to the CPU. The run writes a `summary.json` that names the backend and device each module used.
